identity.name: AK-06
identity.nickname: A hundred hours, with the dial taken off

case.material: stainless steel, also issued in titanium, 18k 5N rose gold and platinum
case.bezel: 26-part case, sapphire front and back, 3 ATM

identity.one_liner: Rexhep Rexhepi's first watch without a tourbillon, and the one where he opened the dial up so the argument would be visible: a hundred-hour reserve in a single jewelled barrel, told by an indicator you wind by hand.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

provenance_events.description: AkriviA unveiled the AK-06 at Baselworld 2017, the first timepiece from Rexhep Rexhepi's workshop to venture beyond the tourbillon. Contemporary coverage recorded availability from September 2017 in steel, titanium, 18k 5N rose gold and platinum, with a stated list price of CHF 79,000 for the steel version.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Phillips Geneva Watch Auction: XXIII, lot 36
provenance_events.description: Movement no. 03 was offered in stainless steel and realised CHF 3,000,000. It is the highest price recorded for the model in this register's evidence, and the first AK-06 the register has held at all — the brand had no card before this one. Phillips does not publish the hammer price or the bid count for this lot, so neither is claimed here.

narrative.story:
Rexhep Rexhepi built AkriviA on tourbillons. The AK-06 is the first watch he made without one, and the reason is not that he lost interest in complications. It is that a hundred hours of power reserve is worth looking at.

So he cut the dial away. The steel version carries a hand-hammered grey open-work dial with a power-reserve indicator at 12 o'clock, and the whole display is a spectacle when you wind the crown or set the time. Underneath it, calibre AK-06 — developed, decorated and assembled in house — holds 100 hours on a single jewelled barrel. Two hundred and sixty-seven components in the movement, hand-finished to Geneva standards including anglage on parts that are never seen.

There is a second idea in the crown. Pull it and two things happen together: the balance stops, and the seconds hand resets to zero. Set the time without the escapement juddering against a running seconds hand. Rexhep Rexhepi calls the balance variable inertia — 10.5mm, free-sprung, four adjustable weights — and it beats at 18,000 vph with a Breguet overcoil.

The case is 26 parts, sapphire front and back, 3 ATM, 41mm across and 9.9mm thick. It was offered in steel, titanium, 18k 5N rose gold and platinum. A dealer account of the steel version records the run as fifty pieces split evenly between steel and titanium. AkriviA does not publish a run size on its own page, so this dossier carries the dealer's figure and names it as the dealer's figure.

The watch that came to Geneva in May 2026 was movement number 03, in steel. It made CHF 3,000,000.
narrative.collector_notes:
The only sourced retail figure in the evidence is CHF 79,000 for the steel version, published at debut in 2017. It is left in the notes rather than converted into the structured MSRP history, because that history stores USD and the only defensible conversion would need a 2017 reference rate that this register has not fetched and will not borrow from a different year. The gap is deliberate: an absent number the register can explain beats a present number it cannot defend.

The maker's own product page states 28 jewels for the movement; Rexhep Rexhepi's page states 39 olive-domed and flat jewels, which counts the case jewels as well as the movement's. The dossier carries the movement figure.

identity.name: AnOrdain Model 1 Midnight Fumé
identity.one_liner: A Thailand-based microbrand built around a single product: a 38mm steel dress watch with a hand-fumed gradient dial. One of the most-cited fumé dials in the microbrand collector world.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the AnOrdain AnOrdain Model 1 Midnight Fumé. Title: File:AnOrdain-01.png.

narrative.story: AnOrdain is the only watch brand in the Time Pop register that is headquartered in northern Thailand. The Model 1 is the brand's single product: a 38mm steel dress watch with a hand-fumed gradient dial (each dial is fumed individually in a small kiln, with the gradient hand-painted in the workshop). The brand is run by a former graphic designer who has said in interviews that the dial-fuming process was the only reason the brand exists. The Model 1 is one of the most-cited fumé-dial watches in the microbrand collector community, with each fumé variant (Midnight, Petrol, Teal, Plum) limited to 50–100 pieces per dial color.
narrative.collector_notes: Each dial is hand-fumed over an open flame, then lacquered. The 38mm case is a manually-finished Chinese-made case sourced through a small Bangkok atelier. The movement is decorated with perlage on the rotor. The brand operates on a direct-order model with a 4-month waitlist per dial variant.

identity.name: Royal Oak Jumbo Extra-Thin
identity.one_liner: The keeper of the 1972 Royal Oak formula — 39mm, 8.1mm, caliber 2121 — retired at the model's 50th birthday.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

provenance_events.description: AP confirmed the steel Jumbo 15202ST would leave production in 2022, to make way for a new reference at the Royal Oak's 50th anniversary. Secondary asking prices climbed roughly 50% on the news.

Audemars Piguet releases the 15202ST, the "Jumbo" Extra-Thin — a 39mm case 8.1mm thick, "Petite Tapisserie" dial, 2121 movement. It becomes the closest modern descendant of the 1972 5402ST and the reference against which all other steel APs are measured.

AP releases the 15202ST as the modern 39mm "Jumbo" Extra-Thin. Hong Kong collectors and the Phillips Hong Kong Watch Auction set the secondary market reference: 15202ST regularly trades at $80k-100k USD on the Hong Kong auction circuit through the 2010s and 2020s.

narrative.story: The 15202 existed to keep the original Royal Oak recipe alive: same 39mm x 8.1mm case as the 1972 5402, same ultra-thin caliber 2121, petite tapisserie dial with the AP monogram restored to 6 o'clock in the 2012 revision. From 2000 to 2022 it was the purist's Royal Oak while the rest of the collection grew and multiplied. AP ended it at the 50th anniversary, handing the format to the 16202 and its new caliber 7121.
narrative.collector_notes: The 2121 has no stop-seconds and a delicate date mechanism — never set the date near midnight, and budget for AP-only servicing. 2012-2022 blue-dial examples are the reference market; earlier dial variants and the 'ST.OO' bracelet generations matter to pricing.

identity.name: Royal Oak Jumbo Extra-Thin
identity.one_liner: The 50th-anniversary Jumbo: the 1972 case dimensions kept, the 50-year-old caliber 2121 finally replaced.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

provenance_events.description: Audemars Piguet releases the 16202ST as the modern-day descendant of the 15202ST. The new caliber 7121 with a full rotor replaces the Frédéric Piguet-derived 2121, marking the first new movement architecture in the "Jumbo" line in fifty years.

Audemars Piguet releases the 16202ST as the modern-day descendant of the 15202ST Jumbo Extra-Thin. The new calibre 7121 (full rotor) replaces the Frédéric Piguet-derived 2121, marking the first new movement architecture in the "Jumbo" line in fifty years. Hong Kong collector demand drives the secondary market at MSRP-plus.

narrative.story: Launched in 2022 for the Royal Oak's 50th anniversary, the 16202ST succeeded the 15202 with the case unchanged at 39mm x 8.1mm and the movement completely new: caliber 7121, larger, with 55 hours of reserve and a quick-set date the 2121 never had. First-year examples carry a '50 years' anniversary rotor. The blue petite tapisserie dial continues the Jumbo lineage unbroken.
narrative.collector_notes: The anniversary rotor marks 2022 production and collectors already sort by it. Waitlists at AP boutiques remain the norm for steel; the smoked-dial and precious-metal variants trade very differently from the standard blue.

identity.name: Royal Oak Offshore

case.bezel: octagonal with eight hexagonal screws, gasket-exposed construction

identity.one_liner: The 1993 original Offshore — 42mm and 15mm thick when that was outrageous, the watch that invented the oversized luxury sports chronograph.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore — the 42mm Diver configuration. The 25721ST is the 1990s Royal Oak Offshore chronograph in the same case family; this is the closest verified CC photograph for the family.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Designer Emmanuel Gueit's own Beast at Phillips Geneva
provenance_events.description: Gueit's personal 25721ST — number 39 of the first 100 pieces, which carry only 'Royal Oak' on the caseback with no Offshore engraving — sold for CHF 102,500 including premium at the Geneva Watch Auction: EIGHT, a record at the time for a steel Offshore.

narrative.story: AP gave 22-year-old designer Emmanuel Gueit the job of making the Royal Oak speak to a younger buyer for its 20th anniversary. His answer, drawn in 1989 and finally launched at Basel 1993, blew the case to 42mm and 15mm thick, exposed the blue gasket between bezel and case, and shielded the 2126/2840 movement against magnetism. Chairman Stephen Urquhart called it 'The Beast'; purists, including Genta himself, hated it. Fewer than 3,000 were made through 2002, and the oversized sports chronograph it invented carried AP for the next three decades.
narrative.collector_notes: The first 100 casebacks without 'Offshore' engraving are the grail sub-variant, with blade-style clasps and screw-secured links. Tropical-turning dials and original strap/bracelet configurations move the price band; D-series serials date the earliest production.

identity.name: Royal Oak Chronograph 41
identity.one_liner: The 2017 Royal Oak chronograph refresh whose silver-and-black panda dial became the collected configuration.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

narrative.story: Marking 20 years of the Royal Oak chronograph in 2017, the 26331ST reworked the 41mm chrono's dial: larger registers pushed outward, cleaner minute track, and a silver grande tapisserie face with black counters — the panda — that instantly became the one to have. Inside remained the compact F. Piguet-based caliber 2385. The reference ran until the 26240 generation with AP's integrated flyback 4401 took over in 2022.
narrative.collector_notes: The panda and reverse-panda dominate demand over the blue and black dials. The 2385 is a modular-free, thin chronograph but lacks flyback and runs at 3Hz — check pusher action and register reset alignment.

identity.name: Royal Oak
identity.one_liner: The 1972 original: Genta's octagonal steel watch at a gold price, the design that saved Audemars Piguet.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: Audemars Piguet CODE 11.59 Chronograph ref. 26393. The closest verified CC-licensed photograph for the 5402ST family; both are modern AP references with the octagonal case DNA.

provenance_events.description: At the 1972 Basel fair, Audemars Piguet launches the 5402ST — designed by Gérald Genta, manufactured by George Watches in les Acacias, with a 39mm steel case and 33 jewels. The press calls it "expensive steel"; collector demand outstrips the 1,000-piece first run within a year.

narrative.story: In 1971 AP asked Gerald Genta for a steel sports watch overnight; the story goes that he delivered the Royal Oak by morning — an octagonal bezel held by eight visible hexagonal screws, inspired by a diver's helmet, on an integrated bracelet. Launched at Basel 1972 at CHF 3,300, roughly ten times a contemporary steel watch, it was ridiculed, then it rescued a company being strangled by the quartz crisis. Production of the 5402 ran to about 1990 across A, B, C and D series, only a few thousand pieces in total, all on the ultra-thin caliber 2121.
narrative.collector_notes: A-series examples (AP monogram at 6, earliest casebacks) are the blue chips; series identification via case numbers is the first authentication step. Dial replacements during AP service were common for decades — original 'petite tapisserie' with correct printing drives the price gap.

identity.one_liner: The current-production resin square descended from the original 1983 DW-5000C that established G-Shock's shock-resistance design.

provenance_events.description: Casio releases the DW-5600 in 1983, two years after the original G-Shock DW-5000. The squared 5600 becomes the most-cited modern G-Shock and the watch most associated with the line's 1980s minimalist design.

narrative.story: Casio's original G-Shock square, the DW-5000C, debuted in April 1983 after engineer Kikuo Ibe's team built and dropped-tested over 200 prototypes to meet a self-imposed 'triple 10' brief: survive a 10-meter fall, resist 10 bar of water pressure, and run 10 years on one battery. The DW-5600 variant carried that shape forward in resin, and Casio has kept the case, screw-back, and three-button layout essentially unchanged for four decades while updating the internal module — the current DW-5600E runs module 3525/3529, introduced in 2023.
narrative.collector_notes: The module number stamped inside the caseback identifies the production era (3229 from 2010, 3525/3529 from 2023); collectors track module changes more closely than case cosmetics, since the shell itself has barely changed.

narrative.story: Designed by Ryusuke Moriai and introduced by Casio in June 1989, the F-91W has stayed in continuous production for over three decades on a formula of low price, long battery life, and an unchanged three-button digital layout. Cumulative production is estimated above 100 million units, making it the best-selling watch ever made. Its ubiquity has cut both ways: the same low cost and simple timer function that made it a favorite everyday watch also led declassified Guantanamo Bay documents to flag it as a marker associated with al-Qaeda bomb-making training.
narrative.collector_notes: Case, dial print, and module have changed little since 1989; collectors distinguish era mainly by the small print on the caseback and country of assembly rather than by any cosmetic revision.

The DS Action Diver 38 takes the company's 60-year DS (Double Security) case-construction heritage and pairs it with the Powermatic 80 (an 80-hour-reserve ETA variant) and a ceramic unidirectional bezel. At 38mm it is one of the few serious dive watches that does not wear oversized on a 6.5-inch wrist. Certina sells the same watch in 43mm and 45.5mm but the 38 is the one Thai collectors cite most often — it is the watch a Bangkok dealer would show a first-time buyer who has outgrown a Seiko.

identity.one_liner: A reissue of the 1960s DS PH200 — one of the most-cited mid-century skin-divers, now with a Powermatic 80 and ceramic bezel.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

narrative.story: The original Certina DS PH200 was issued in 1967 and was the watch Issacar Andraos wore to the deepest dive a human had made in 1969. The 2019 reissue takes the case silhouette, the dial layout, and the bezel hash-mark pattern, and pairs them with the modern Powermatic 80. The result is a watch that reads as a 1960s skin-diver in the hand and behaves as a 2020s daily on the wrist. The DS case construction (a second gasket inside the caseback) was the original selling point in 1967 and remains the technical answer to the question "is this watch actually water-resistant to 200m?" — yes, with a margin.
narrative.collector_notes: The bezel insert is ceramic, not aluminium, which is the most-cited 2019-reissue upgrade. The dial has the original "turtle" markers and a 6 o'clock date. There is no helium escape valve; this is a recreational dive watch, not a saturation watch.

identity.name: Simplicity

movement.caliber: in-house manual-wind, hand-finished entirely by Dufour

case.material: platinum, yellow gold, pink gold, or white gold

identity.one_liner: A time-only watch made almost entirely by one watchmaker's hands, built to demonstrate that traditional Geneva finishing techniques could still be executed to their original standard rather than approximated by machine.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

narrative.story: Philippe Dufour introduced the Simplicity in 2000 after decades restoring and complicating watches for other Geneva houses, stripping his own design down to hours, minutes, and a small seconds so the movement finishing had nowhere to hide. Every visible surface, from the anglage on the bridges to the black-polished steel of the small parts, is finished by hand using techniques Dufour learned from restoring 19th-century pocket watches rather than from CNC-assisted modern production. Annual output has stayed in the low double digits for its entire run, and Dufour has personally trained several of the watchmakers now working under their own names as independents, including Rexhep Rexhepi.
narrative.collector_notes: Case metal and the rare stainless-steel examples define most of the price spread; dial layout and finishing are consistent across the run, so provenance and documented ownership history carry unusual weight for a watch this recently made, given how closely the collector community tracks individual serial numbers.

case.material: stainless steel (also in titanium, rose gold)

identity.one_liner: The 1941 Remontoire is the Grönefeld brothers' signature — a hand-finished in-house movement with an 8-second constant-force remontoire, in a 40mm steel case that is the most-cited modern Dutch independent watch.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the Grönefeld Grönefeld 1941 Remontoire. Title: File:Anna-Lena Grönefeld, Damen-Tennis-Bundesliga Moers, 02.jpg.

narrative.story: The Grönefeld brothers (Tim and Bart) are third-generation watchmakers from Oldenzaal, Netherlands, who established their brand in 2008. The 1941 Remontoire is the watch that put them on the global map: a 40mm steel case containing an in-house manual-wind movement with an 8-second remontoire — a constant-force mechanism that re-tensions the mainspring every 8 seconds, dramatically improving rate stability. The 1941 is named after the brothers' grandfather, who was a horology instructor in 1941. Production is roughly 12 pieces per year. The 1941 is the most-cited modern Dutch independent watch in international collector circles.
narrative.collector_notes: The 8-second remontoire uses a small auxiliary spring that is wound and released every 8 seconds, providing a constant force to the escapement. The main plate of the movement is hand-finished with a "frosted" texture that takes roughly 4 hours per movement. Production is roughly 12 pieces per year. The brand is among the most-awarded independents of the past decade.

identity.one_liner: A 46mm automatic with a 7-day power reserve, descended from 1940s observation watches built for military navigators rather than pilots' wrists.

brand_context.label: Iconic mainstream leaders
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: IWC Big Pilot Saint-Exupéry Edition — the same 46mm Big Pilot case family as the IW501001. The IW501001 is the steel Big Pilot with the Pellaton winding system.

provenance_events.description: IWC reissues the 1940s Beobachtungsuhr (B-Uhr) pilot's watch as the Big Pilot's Watch 5002 (later 5007, 5010) in 2002. The 46.2mm case, conical crown, and onion-style hands establish the modern "Big Pilot" aesthetic that runs to the present.

narrative.story: IWC's Big Pilot lineage traces to 1940s observation watches like the Caliber 52 T.S.C., a 55mm pocket-watch-sized instrument built for military navigators who needed a large, highly legible dial rather than a watch meant to be worn during flight. IWC reintroduced the concept as a wearable wristwatch in 2002, and the current Big Pilot's Watch keeps the oversized crown and dial legibility of the original while adding a 7-day power reserve indicator — a feature the 1940s version, read at a desk rather than worn, never needed to solve.
narrative.collector_notes: Confirm the exact movement generation (52010 vs. 52110 vs. later updates), since power-reserve indicator position and case-back engraving changed across updates without any change to the outward case design.

narrative.story: IWC launched the Ingenieur in 1955 as reference 666, an anti-magnetic watch built for engineers and professionals working near electrical equipment. In 1976, designer Gérald Genta reworked it into the Ingenieur SL reference 1832 — a 40mm case nicknamed 'Jumbo' for its size at the time, with an integrated bracelet, a screw-down bezel with five visible recesses, rubber shock buffers, and a soft-iron inner case for magnetic shielding. Genta designed the SL the same year as the Patek Philippe Nautilus and six years after his Audemars Piguet Royal Oak — three integrated-bracelet steel sports watches from one designer within a single decade. IWC's 2023 Ingenieur Automatic 40 revives the SL's five-recess bezel and integrated-bracelet silhouette directly, after several intervening Ingenieur generations had moved toward more conventional round cases.
narrative.collector_notes: Compare the new Ingenieur's bezel recess count and bracelet link shape directly against the 1976 SL if homage accuracy matters to you — IWC marketed this relaunch explicitly on faithfulness to the Genta original, so deviations are more collector-relevant here than on a line without that direct lineage claim.

identity.one_liner: A wearable mechanical alarm — a second mainspring and a hammer strike the caseback at the hour set on the inner disc.

brand_context.label: Iconic mainstream leaders
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

provenance_events.description: Jaeger-LeCoultre's Memovox — "memory of voice" — is the first watch with a mechanical alarm complication, in a case designed by the brand's in-house Renaud & Papi studio. The Polaris Memovox reissue (1968 / 2018) and the Master Ultra Thin Memovox keep the line current.

narrative.story: Jaeger-LeCoultre introduced the Memovox in 1950, one of the first mechanical wristwatches with a built-in alarm — a second mainspring drives a hammer that strikes the caseback at a time set by an inner rotating disc. The first self-winding version followed in 1956 with caliber 815. JLC extended the idea to tool watches with the 1959 Deep Sea and the 1965 Polaris, which used a patented triple-case-back construction so the alarm could still be heard underwater; JLC revisited that design directly with a 2008 Memovox Tribute to Polaris reissue. The alarm mechanism is a genuine mechanical achievement rather than a styling exercise: it requires an entirely separate spring barrel and striking train alongside the timekeeping movement, in a case no larger than an ordinary three-hand watch.
narrative.collector_notes: JLC has renamed and re-cased the Memovox several times across relaunches (plain Memovox, Master Control Memovox, Tribute to Polaris), so confirm the exact current reference and movement generation with an authorized dealer rather than assuming a name maps to one fixed specification. On used examples, test that the alarm actually winds, sets, and strikes audibly — alarm mechanisms see far less routine servicing attention than the timekeeping side and are the first thing to fail quietly.

narrative.story: The Reverso was created in 1931 after polo players in India asked Paris watch dealer César de Trey for a wristwatch that could survive the sport. De Trey brought the problem to Jacques-David LeCoultre, whose engineer René-Alfred Chauvot patented a case that slides and flips within a metal carrier, turning the crystal to face the wrist during play. The reversible case outlived its original purpose and became one of the defining Art Deco watch shapes of the twentieth century; Jaeger-LeCoultre has kept some version of the Reverso in the catalog almost continuously since.
narrative.collector_notes: The flat caseback is a common surface for engraving, which most collectors treat as a value reducer unless the engraving has personal or historical significance. JLC has changed the Reverso Classic line's case proportions and calibers across several relaunches, so confirm which generation and movement a given piece carries rather than assuming continuity across years.

identity.one_liner: Two independent balance wheels regulating each other through resonance rather than a shared gear train, shown on a twin-dial layout that displays two time zones.

brand_context.label: Independent & enthusiast

media.caption: JLC Master Geographic ref. Q4128420. The closest verified CC-licensed photograph for the F.P. Journe Résonance; both are haute horlogerie complications with travel/dual-time functions.

provenance_events.description: A Souscription-series Chronomètre à Résonance, No. 007 of the original 20-piece founding-client edition from circa 2000, sold for $13,922,000 at Phillips New York Watch Auction XIV, the highest price ever paid at commercial auction for a 21st-century wristwatch and for any watch by an independent watchmaker.

narrative.story: The Résonance was one of the first watches F.P. Journe produced under his own name, a subscription series of twenty pieces offered to founding clients around 2000 to help finance the fledgling company before it built the boutique network that supports it today. The mechanical premise is unusual: two separate balance wheels, each with its own escapement, are placed close enough together that they entrain each other through physical resonance, a phenomenon Journe used to improve rate stability rather than just as a display gimmick. The dial's twin sub-dials read two time zones, one for each balance train.
narrative.collector_notes: Souscription-series pieces from the original circa-2000 run are a distinct, far scarcer population than the standard-production Résonance that followed; collectors treat them as effectively a different watch for valuation purposes despite sharing the model name.

identity.one_liner: The 2012 update to the original 1999 Datograph, adding a power-reserve display to the flyback chronograph movement collectors already rated among the finest column-wheel calibers made.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie

provenance_events.description: The Datograph debuts at Basel 1999 with the calibre L951.1 — the first in-house chronograph from A. Lange & Söhne, and a movement that defines the next two decades of chronograph collecting. The "Up/Down" power-reserve version follows in 2012.

narrative.story: The original 1999 Datograph put Lange's in-house L951.1 column-wheel flyback chronograph on the map, hand-finished to a standard most chronograph houses reserved for time-only movements. The Up/Down update shown here, introduced at SIHH 2012, adds a power-reserve indicator alongside the running minute counter, giving the L951.6 a longer 60-hour reserve without changing the case proportions that made the original legible and symmetrical.
narrative.collector_notes: Collectors check the jumping minute counter for a clean, instantaneous snap rather than a lagging creep, since the snail cam that drives it is a known service point. identity.one_liner: Lange's digital-jump hours-and-minutes display, driven by a patented constant-force escapement that releases stored energy once every sixty seconds to advance the discs cleanly.

provenance_events.description: A. Lange & Söhne's Zeitwerk debuts as a digital-display watch with three jumping numerals and a constant-force escapement. The piece becomes the brand's most-photographed haute horlogerie statement — the "piano" numerals visible across the dial at every angle.

narrative.story: The Zeitwerk, introduced in 2009, moved Lange into digital time display without giving up mechanical construction: hours and minutes jump on discs rather than sweep on hands, timed by a remontoir d'egalite that stores and releases energy in one-second increments so the discs advance instantly rather than dragging. narrative.collector_notes: The jump mechanism draws down power quickly; collectors check that the power-reserve indicator and the jump action stay synchronized, since a worn remontoir spring shows up first as a hesitant or double jump rather than a reserve-display error.

identity.published_model_name: Triple Detent Constant Force One Minute Tourbillon Chronometer
identity.name: Triple Detent Constant Force Tourbillon Chronometer

case.bezel: hinged front bezel with constant-force spiral

identity.one_liner: A pocket chronometer that puts a tourbillon regulator behind a constant-force escapement — and is believed to be the only watch ever made to combine the two. Circa 1860, 56mm yellow gold, movement no. 12, ex-Harlow Shapley.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

provenance_events.description: Louis Jean Richard, born in Le Locle in 1812, earned a gold medal from the Société d'Émulation for a chronometer with free escapement and constant force. He bought astronomical instruments in Paris to conduct his own celestial observations and regulated his watches by stellar movement; his workshop was fitted with an ice chamber and an oven to test performance at extreme temperatures.
Richard exhibited a marine chronometer at the Great Exhibition of 1851 and was awarded an A Prize Medal.

The watch last appeared at auction at Sotheby's New York on 30 October 1990, lot 448. Phillips records that it subsequently belonged to Harlow Shapley, Director of the Harvard College Observatory and Emeritus Professor of Astronomy at Harvard, president of eight national scientific organizations, author of Of Stars and Men, and laureate of the Pius XI Prize for Science and Humanity.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Phillips Geneva Watch Auction: XXIII, lot 108
provenance_events.description: The watch sold for CHF 3,968,000 after 46 bids. Phillips describes it as the only known example combining Richard's constant force escapement with a tourbillon regulator, and notes that a separate finely finished regulator by Richard dated 1842 is preserved at the Musée International d'Horlogerie. The tourbillon frame is released by a latch and a slide lever between 5 and 6 o'clock, and an A-M lever (arrêt-marche) locks the third wheel so the carriage can be removed for adjustment without releasing the mainspring.

narrative.story:
Two ideas that were never married, married in one watch.

The constant-force escapement, by Phillips's account of Richard, ensures the balance receives the same push through the whole mainspring run instead of more at the top and less at the bottom. The tourbillon cancels the gravitational error a balance picks up as it rotates. Do both and the arithmetic gets very good indeed. Almost nobody did both. Phillips describes this watch as the only known example in the history of watchmaking that combines Richard's constant force escapement with a tourbillon regulator.

Richard built it in the 1840s, in Le Locle, at the height of nineteenth-century chronometry. The movement carries a three-arm bimetallic compensation balance with gold timing screws, free-sprung and fitted with a helical hairspring. The carriage is half polished and half matte, and its three detents do what detents have always done: rest, impulse, disengagement. Fourteen large ruby jewels, frosted gilt plates, a matte steel bridge. The movement is engraved Invenit et Fecit — he invented it and he made it.

The engineering detail worth stopping on is the A-M lever. Arrêt-marche, stop and go, marked A through M on a second lever beneath the hinged front bezel. It locks the tooth of the third wheel so the tourbillon carriage can be lifted out for adjustment without letting the mainspring run down. In a lever-escapement watch, servicing meant releasing the spring. Here, the watch can be regulated while it stays going.

It surfaced once before, at Sotheby's New York in 1990. After that it belonged to an astronomer. Harlow Shapley ran the Harvard College Observatory, spent a career measuring how far away things were, and wrote five books and nearly five hundred papers, among them Of Stars and Men. He sold it in Geneva in May 2026 after 46 bids, and the price was CHF 3,968,000.
narrative.collector_notes:
There is no market for this object in the ordinary sense and the register does not pretend otherwise. One watch, one known example, one sale in living memory. The comp on this dossier is marked not comparable on purpose: a unique object cannot establish a range, and nothing is estimated from it. The comparable figure is deliberately absent rather than borrowed from a neighbouring pocket chronometer.

The reference reads 'Triple Detent Constant Force' because Richard published no reference numbers and this is the name the auction house prints. There is no retail price, no catalogue, no production run — the register carries an empty MSRP history rather than inventing one.

variant_sales.condition: Phillips Geneva Watch Auction: XXIII, lot 108. Circa 1860, 18k yellow gold, 56mm, movement no. 12, case no. 11846 12, dial and movement signed, movement further engraved 'Invenit et Fecit'. Hammer CHF 3,200,000; sold CHF 3,968,000 (converted at the ECB reference rate for 2026-05-08) after 46 bids. Provenance: Sotheby's New York, 30 October 1990, lot 448; thence by descent from Harlow Shapley, Director of the Harvard College Observatory. Marked NOT COMPARABLE because Phillips describes it as the only known example in the history of watchmaking: one sale is a data point, not a price series, and nothing may be estimated from it. Literature: Revue Française de l'Horlogerie Ancienne no. 8 (1980), pp. 52-60.

provenance_events.description: MB&F's Legacy Machine 101 (LM101) debuts as the brand's most "classical" piece: a suspended balance wheel above a sub-dial, with a 45mm case and an in-house movement. MB&F positions it as a "watchmaker's watch" — the simplest, most personal piece in the Horological Machine catalogue.

narrative.story: The Legacy Machine 101 (LM101) is Max Büsser's tribute to 19th-century pocket-watch chronometer design, updated to a wristwatch format. The signature is the 14mm balance wheel suspended above the dial on a vertical arch — a hand-engraved bridge of polished steel. The result is a watch that looks like a small mechanical planet. The LM101 was followed by the LM101 MB&F × H. Moser in 2020 (a H. Moser × MB&F collaboration), and the LM101 EVO in 2022. The original LM101 ran 2014-2018 in white gold; the 2022 reissue is in steel, titanium, and limited platinum.

case.bezel: fixed stainless with engraved "Clous de Paris" pattern

identity.one_liner: The Maurice Lacroix Aikon is the Swiss integrated-bracelet sports watch Asian collectors buy instead of an entry-level Royal Oak — the casework is the same supplier as AP's steel sports line.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the Maurice Lacroix Maurice Lacroix Aikon Automatic 42. Title: File:2023100802 Maurice Lacroix schraegseitlich links.jpg.

narrative.story: The Aikon is Maurice Lacroix's most-photographed case — a 42mm steel integrated-bracelet sports watch with the brand's "Clous de Paris" hobnail pattern on the bezel. The line is the brand's most successful in Asia, where it sells as the Swiss alternative to an entry-level Audemars Piguet Royal Oak. The case uses the same case-supplier (Les Artisans Boîtiers) that supplies Audemars Piguet's steel sports line — which is why the finishing reads as AP-adjacent at one-fifth the price. Maurice Lacroix is one of the last Swiss independent-brand holdouts that has not been acquired by a group.
narrative.collector_notes: The Clous de Paris pattern is hobnail-engraved on the bezel, not stamped — visible under loupe. The bracelet is integrated, no end-links, with brushed and polished surfaces. The movement is decorated (Geneva stripes, blued screws) but not COSC certified.

identity.name: Mido Multifort TV Big Date
identity.one_liner: The Mido Multifort TV Big Date is the watch Asian collectors reach for when they want a TV-shaped dial, a 80-hour movement, and a price that does not make the watch the most expensive thing in the room.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the Mido Mido Multifort TV Big Date. Title: File:Mido (Egyptian Footballer).png.

narrative.story: The Multifort was Mido's 1930s line and the TV-shaped case (the horizontal TV-screen silhouette, not the boob-tube one) is the line's signature. The 2022 Big Date reissue pairs the original 1970s silhouette with the modern Caliber 80 (an 80-hour-reserve automatic) and a 12 o'clock big date. Mido is the Swatch Group brand that sits between Tissot and Longines in the hierarchy, and the Multifort is the line Asian collectors cite most often. The TV shape is the most-photographed Mido case in the brand's modern output.

identity.name: Mido Ocean Star 600 Chronometer
identity.one_liner: A COSC-certified 600m dive watch from the Swatch Group — chronometer-grade at sub-$2,000, with the case construction Mido has been refining since the 1940s.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the Mido Mido Ocean Star 600 Chronometer. Title: File:Mido-Ocean-Star-GMT.jpg.

narrative.story: The Ocean Star line has been Mido's dive watch since 1944. The 600 Chronometer is the modern extreme: a 43.5mm steel case rated to 600m, a COSC-certified Caliber 80, and a ceramic unidirectional bezel. Mido sells very few of these relative to Tissot and Longines — the 600 is the watch the dealer brings out when the customer has said "show me something serious, but I am not paying Omega money." Mido's positioning in the Swatch Group is the value play just below Longines, and the Ocean Star 600 is the most-cited argument for that positioning.
narrative.collector_notes: COSC certification means the movement has passed the Swiss chronometer test in five positions over 15 days. The 600m water resistance is double the ISO 6425 dive watch minimum, and the case uses a helium escape valve at 9 o'clock for saturation diving. The dial has applied indices and a date at 3 o'clock.

identity.name: Speedmaster Professional
identity.one_liner: The asymmetric-case, twisted-lug reference NASA qualified for spaceflight in 1965 and the exact configuration Buzz Aldrin wore outside his spacesuit on the Apollo 11 moonwalk.

brand_context.label: Iconic mainstream leaders
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the Omega Speedmaster Professional. Title: File:Omega Speedmaster compilation pp01.jpg.

provenance_events.description: Buzz Aldrin wore his Speedmaster 105.012 strapped over his spacesuit cuff during the Apollo 11 lunar EVA, making it the first watch worn on the Moon. Neil Armstrong left his own 105.012 inside the Lunar Module as a backup timer after the LM's own clock had failed testing, so his watch never went outside on this mission.

narrative.story: Introduced in 1964, the 105.012 was the first Speedmaster to carry the asymmetric case with crown guards, twisted lugs, and the 'Professional' designation — the case shape still used on the Moonwatch today. It is the exact reference configuration that passed NASA's 1965 qualification testing for extravehicular use on caliber 321. Aldrin's own 105.012, worn on the lunar surface in July 1969, was shipped to the Smithsonian in the early 1970s and went missing in transit; it has never been recovered, making it one of the most valuable unlocated objects in watch collecting.
narrative.collector_notes: Confirm caliber 321, not the later 861 that arrived with the visually similar 145.012 in 1968, check dial and hand execution against known period variants, and treat any redial or relumed hands as a material condition issue given how heavily surviving examples have been serviced over sixty years.

narrative.story: Costume designer Lindy Hemming moved Bond from Rolex to Omega for GoldenEye (1995), reasoning that Rolex had become too flashy for a character with a Royal Navy background; Pierce Brosnan wore the quartz Seamaster 300M ref 2541.80 on screen in that film. Omega followed with an automatic, COSC-certified version of the same watch, ref 2531.80 on Caliber 1120, which Brosnan wore in Tomorrow Never Dies (1997), The World Is Not Enough (1999), and Die Another Day (2002) - three films, making it the reference most associated with the Brosnan Bond years even though it wasn't the one on screen in GoldenEye itself. Daniel Craig's Casino Royale replaced it with the co-axial 2220.80.
narrative.collector_notes: Confirm the bezel insert, crystal, and helium escape valve are original - all three are common service-replacement parts on a reference that's been worn and serviced continuously since the 1990s. 'First batch' 1993-1995 examples are tracked closely on Omega collector forums for small bracelet and end-link differences.

case.bezel: steel bezel with black tachymeter scale

identity.one_liner: The first Speedmaster reference, introduced in 1957 with a 39mm steel case and the first tachymeter scale printed on a wristwatch bezel rather than the dial.

brand_context.label: Iconic mainstream leaders
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the Omega Speedmaster. Title: File:Omega Speedmaster Schumacher Edition .jpeg.

provenance_events.description: A CK2915-1 (lot 53) hammers for CHF 3,115,500 (about $3.4M USD), the highest price ever paid for an Omega at auction, against a pre-sale estimate of CHF 80,000-120,000.

Watch researcher Jose Perez publishes evidence that the record-priced CK2915-1 sold by Phillips in 2021 is an assembly of non-original parts; Omega later confirmed the finding and identified three former employees, including its former museum head, as responsible.

narrative.story: Introduced in 1957 alongside the Railmaster and Seamaster 300 as part of what dealers now call the 'Broad Arrow' trilogy, the CK2915 was the first watch sold under the Speedmaster name and the first wristwatch with its tachymeter scale printed on a fixed steel bezel instead of the dial. It runs the manual-wind caliber 321, a Lemania-based column-wheel chronograph that Omega continued using through the mid-1960s Speedmasters worn during NASA's Gemini and early Apollo programs. Omega made it in three execution batches between 1957 and 1959, in low numbers, before replacing it with the CK2998 — the rarest regular-production Speedmaster reference, and one of the most closely examined watches in the vintage market since a widely publicized 2021 auction sale was later found to involve non-original parts.
narrative.collector_notes: The three execution batches (2915-1, -2, -3) differ in bezel, hand, and dial details that collectors use to date a given watch within the 1957-1959 run; caliber 321 originality and correct broad-arrow hands are the standard checkpoints. The reference's most publicized recent sale — a CHF 3,115,500 Phillips hammer in November 2021 — was found in 2023 to be an assembly of non-original parts fitted by former Omega staff, so independent verification matters more on this reference than an Extract from the Archives alone.

provenance_events.description: Wally Schirra wears his personal Omega Speedmaster ref CK2998 aboard Mercury-Atlas 8 (Sigma 7), making it the first Omega worn in space, five years before the Moonwatch story of Buzz Aldrin on the lunar surface.

narrative.story: Wally Schirra wore his own Omega Speedmaster ref CK2998 on his wrist during Mercury-Atlas 8 on October 3, 1962, three years before Omega's Speedmaster was formally qualified by NASA for spaceflight and five years before the Apollo 11 Moonwatch story took over the marketing narrative. Omega introduced the First Omega in Space in 2012 as a faithful-dimension tribute: a 39.7mm case matching the CK2998, a hand-wound Caliber 1861 chronograph, a matte black dial, a black anodized aluminum tachymeter bezel, and a sapphire crystal in place of the original's Hesalite. Each caseback carries a unique serial number and the inscription 'THE FIRST OMEGA IN SPACE' with the mission date, though Omega never stated a fixed edition size before discontinuing the reference in late 2020.
narrative.collector_notes: The FOIS was leather-strap only - Omega never offered a steel bracelet option for this reference, unlike most other Speedmaster Professional variants. It's numbered but not officially limited; on full-set examples, check that the caseback serial matches the warranty card.

provenance_events.person_or_event: NASA Silver Snoopy Award to Omega
provenance_events.description: NASA presents Omega with the Silver Snoopy Award, recognizing the Speedmaster's role in calculating the critical engine burns that brought Apollo 13 home after its oxygen tank explosion.
Omega introduces the Speedmaster Silver Snoopy Award 50th Anniversary on the exact 50th anniversary of the original 1970 award, positioning it as a special (not limited) ongoing model.

narrative.story: NASA gave Omega the Silver Snoopy Award on October 5, 1970, for the Speedmaster's part in timing the engine burns that returned the Apollo 13 crew safely to Earth after their oxygen tank exploded. Omega marked the award's 50th anniversary on the same date in 2020 with this reference: a manual-wind Caliber 3861 chronograph in a 42mm case, a solid Ag925 silver dial, a navy ceramic bezel, and a sapphire caseback where an animated Snoopy figure and rotating Earth disc move while the chronograph runs. Unlike Omega's earlier, numbered 2003 Snoopy edition, this piece was explicitly announced as a special model rather than a limited run, and has stayed in the catalog since.
narrative.collector_notes: Confirm the caseback module still cycles correctly on a pre-owned example - the rotating Earth disc and swinging Snoopy figure are linked to the chronograph gear train and can stick if the watch sat unused for years. Because it isn't a numbered limited edition, there's no early/late production variant to chase; specification has stayed consistent since 2020.

identity.name: Speedmaster Professional
identity.one_liner: The 1969-1973 Speedmaster Professional with the caliber 861 — the reference worn on Apollo 11 and the first Moon landing.

narrative.story: The 145.022-69 is the Speedmaster Professional that Buzz Aldrin wore on the Moon on July 20, 1969 (Neil Armstrong's Speedmaster was left on the Lunar Module; the 145.012 Aldrin left on the lunar surface is now at the Smithsonian). The caliber 861 is the cam-driven chronograph that replaced the 321 in 1968; it has a 45-minute counter and a 12-hour totalizer but is otherwise simpler. The 145.022-69 is the most-cited Moon watch and the most-cited Speedmaster in the secondary market, with the "Pre-Moon" nickname identifying any 105.003, 105.012, or 145.012 produced before the 1969 lunar landing.
narrative.collector_notes: The 145.022-69 has the "STEP" dial (the T in SPEEDMASTER is on the same line as PROFESSIONAL). The 145.022-69 is sometimes called the "Transitional" because it has the 861 caliber but the 105-series case design.

provenance_events.description: Buzz Aldrin wears his Omega Speedmaster Professional on the lunar surface during Apollo 11. NASA's qualification of the Speedmaster in 1965, after testing by astronaut candidates in a Houston simulation, makes it the first watch worn on the Moon.

Omega releases the Speedmaster Professional with the calibre 1861 — the manual-wind successor to the 861, running 1996-2021. The 1861 is the most-cited Speedmaster of the modern era and a steady secondary-market item through the Asian ADs.

narrative.story: Caliber 1861 replaced the 861 in the Speedmaster Professional line in 1997, a finishing and reliability update to a movement architecture that traces back to the manually wound caliber 321 NASA qualified for Apollo. Omega kept the 1861 essentially unchanged through reference 311.30.42.30.01.005, the hesalite-crystal Moonwatch, for 24 years — the longest run of any Speedmaster movement — before introducing the co-axial-escapement caliber 3861 in 2021 and phasing the 1861 out of the catalog.
narrative.collector_notes: Check dial print generation and hand luminova color against known transitional periods, whether the caseback is the closed steel Seahorse medallion (hesalite version) or a sapphire display back (a different, later reference), and service history — manual-wind chronographs see more winding-crown and pusher wear than automatics.

identity.name: Nautilus
identity.one_liner: The 1976 original: Genta's porthole Nautilus, a 42mm steel watch priced like gold.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: Jumbo Nautilus ref. 3700/1A — the original 1976 Genta porthole, not the 5711. The 3700 is what the 5711 inherited the silhouette from.

provenance_events.description: Gérald Genta draws the Nautilus in a single night after Basel director René Benabès commissions a steel sports watch that could compete with AP's Royal Oak. The horizontal-grooved dial, porthole bezel, and integrated bracelet define luxury-steel for the next fifty years.

Patek Philippe releases the 3700/1A "Jumbo" at Basel — the first luxury steel sports watch from the Stern family. The JLC-powered caliber 28-255 is JLC's thinnest automatic with date, but launch reception is muted: "a watch like a ship's porthole" was not the praise Patek hoped for.

narrative.story: Gerald Genta sketched the Nautilus during a Basel fair lunch, borrowing the proportions of a ship's porthole: a two-part case sealed by lateral 'ears', an embossed horizontal-relief dial, an integrated bracelet. Patek launched it in 1976 as the 3700/1, a 42mm steel watch priced against gold dress watches — the second act of the Genta steel-luxury idea after the Royal Oak. The 28-255 C inside is the same ultra-thin JLC 920 base AP used in the 5402. Production ran, with bracelet revisions, until about 1990.
narrative.collector_notes: Early first-series examples with correct dials and unstretched original bracelets carry the money; service dials and swapped clasps are common after five decades. The market corrected sharply after 2022 — recent New York results sit far below what identical watches asked at the peak.

identity.name: Nautilus
identity.one_liner: The steel Nautilus whose 2021 discontinuation set off the largest price run in modern watch collecting.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: Nautilus in steel with the blue embossed dial and date at 3 — the 5711/1A configuration, identified from the dial, case and bracelet rather than from a marked reference.

provenance_events.description: Patek Philippe confirmed the end of the steel 5711/1A-010 after a 15-year run, at the peak of its waitlist era. Secondary asking prices jumped within days and roughly doubled over the following year.
Antiquorum's Monaco sale offered the first olive-green 5711/1A-014 months after its debut; it sold at a large multiple of the $34,893 list price, confirming the post-discontinuation frenzy.

The 5711/1A replaces the 3700/1A as the entry steel Nautilus, with centre seconds and a slightly thicker case. It looks like a quiet update; for the next fifteen years it becomes the watch world's most-cited waitlist case study.

Patek announces the last 5711 — a Tiffany-blue-dial collaboration, retailed only at Tiffany. Of 170 pieces, the final example sells for $6.5M at Phillips in December 2021 (with the final example at the Phillips 2024 New York Watch Auction X realizing $4.35M for the John Player Special).

Patek retires the 5711/1A at the end of 2021, replaced by the 5811/1G-001 in white gold. The 5711's exit turns what was a multi-year waitlist into a closed chapter and pushes aftermarket prices above the Tiffany-blue sale price.

A Patek 5711/1A-010 sells for HK$7.5M (US$960k) at the Phillips Hong Kong Watch Auction in June 2019 — the highest auction price for a 5711 at the time, and a leading indicator of the Asian market's appetite for steel Nautilus.

narrative.story: The 5711 arrived in 2006 for the Nautilus 30th anniversary, a slimmed 40mm reading of Gerald Genta's 1976 porthole design. It carried caliber 324 S C until 2019, then 26-330 S C for its final two years. In January 2021 Patek killed it while demand was at its most absurd, sent a one-year olive-green dial out as the finale, and turned a five-figure sports watch into the defining hype asset of the era. Secondary prices peaked well into six figures in early 2022 and have retraced hard since, as the Phillips results show.
narrative.collector_notes: Caliber generation matters: 2019-2021 examples run the 26-330 S C with a stop-seconds function the 324 S C lacks, so check the certificate against the movement. Full sets carry a real premium, and buyers today are pricing against the 2022 peak, not retail.

provenance_events.description: The first 5711/1A-018 sold for $6,503,500 including fees, roughly 124 times its $52,635 retail price, with proceeds to The Nature Conservancy. It closed the 5711 story eleven months after the reference was discontinued.

narrative.story: Patek's send-off for the 5711 and a nod to 170 years of retail partnership with Tiffany & Co.: 170 pieces with a Tiffany Blue lacquer dial, double-signed on dial and caseback, allocated only through Tiffany boutiques in December 2021. narrative.collector_notes: The dial and caseback double stamp is the whole game; paperwork tracing the Tiffany allocation matters more here than on any standard Nautilus. Later examples have changed hands far below the charity result, which was a one-off number with a philanthropic premium built in.

provenance_events.description: The 5980/1A is Patek's first Nautilus chronograph — a single sub-dial "small seconds"-style 60-minute counter at 6, caliber CH 28-520. The form factor becomes the basis for the future 5990 travel-time chrono.

narrative.story: The 5980/1A-001 of 2006 gave the Nautilus its first chronograph, thirty years into the model's life. narrative.collector_notes: The -001 gradient dial and the -014 blue are distinct markets; the mono-counter takes explanation but is the reference's signature. Sticky chronograph pushers are the common service tell.

provenance_events.description: Patek adds the Travel Time complication to the Nautilus chrono case — a dual time display with day/night indicators at 3 and 9, flyback chronograph, on the CH 28-520 C FUS caliber. The 5990/1A becomes the most-asked steel Nautilus of the late 2010s.

Patek releases the 5990/1A — the Travel Time Chronograph version of the 5980, with a dual-time display and a flyback chronograph. The 5990/1A becomes the most-cited Asian Patek chronograph of the 2010s, with a multi-year waitlist at Hong Kong ADs.

narrative.story: Introduced in 2014, the 5990/1A packed Patek's Travel Time module — skeletonized home-time hand, day/night windows, pushers in the left case flank — onto the flyback chronograph base of the 5980. narrative.collector_notes: The four case-flank pushers make polishing history easy to spot; check the analog date sub-register at 12 tracks local time after any service. The -001 and -011 dials are different markets.

identity.name: Perpetual Calendar Split-Seconds Chronograph
identity.one_liner: The 5004 is the perpetual calendar split-seconds chronograph that defined the modern Patek grand complication — produced 1995-2012, the last hand-wound perpetual chrono before the 5204 took over.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

narrative.story: The 5004 is a Lemania base caliber (Lemania 2320) modified by Patek, with a perpetual calendar, split-seconds, and a leap-year indicator. The split-seconds (rattrapante) lets the wearer time two events that start together but end at different times — useful for race timing, photography, and stopping a chronograph without losing the original reading. The 5004G (white gold, 1995) and 5004J (yellow gold, 1996) and 5004R (rose gold) and 5004P (platinum) are all four produced 1995-2012, with the platinum at 250 examples. The 5004 is the most-cited split-seconds perpetual of the 1990s-2010s.
narrative.collector_notes: The 5004P is the grail: 250 examples, and the only platinum Patek with both a perpetual and a split-seconds. Look for the Breguet numerals, the small seconds at 9, the 30-minute counter at 3, the day/date sub-dials at 6.

identity.name: Annual Calendar
identity.one_liner: The 1996 Annual Calendar — Patek invented the complication in 1996, and the 5035J is the watch that made it accessible. The reference that started the entire annual-calendar category.

brand_context.label: Haute horlogerie
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

narrative.story: Patek launched the annual calendar in 1996 with the 5035. The mechanism "remembers" the length of every month except February in leap year — it needs a single correction once a year, on March 1. The 5035 was the first annual calendar in series production, and the complication has since been adopted by Rolex (Sky-Dweller 2012, via the Saros system) and Vacheron. The 5035J ran 1996-2003 before the 5146 replaced it. The annual calendar is the rare Patek complication that is both a watchmaking milestone and an everyday-wearable watch.

narrative.story: The 5170J is the reference that retired the Lemania-derived caliber that Patek had used for fifty years. The CH 29-535 PS is the first chronograph caliber fully designed in-house, and it is also the first with a column wheel visible through the case back. narrative.collector_notes: The CH 29-535 PS has six patents on the chronograph mechanism alone, including the tooth profile of the column wheel. The 5170 is the reference a collector cites when they want to argue Patek's chronograph chronograph engineering is real, not decorative.

identity.name: Annual Calendar Regulator
identity.one_liner: The Patek regulator — the only regulator-style watch in Patek's modern catalogue, with a single hour hand, a separate minute hand, and a sub-seconds subdial. The quietest Patek complications piece.

provenance_events.description: Patek Philippe releases the 5235 as the brand's only regulator-style watch — a single hour hand at 6, a central minute hand, an annual calendar with day/date/month in a sub-dial at 6.

narrative.story: The 5235 is Patek's only modern regulator — a layout where the hour is on a sub-dial and only the minute is on a central hand. Patek has long resisted the regulator style (which is associated with German watchmaking) but in 2011 they made one for the Asian market's preference for asymmetric dial layouts.
narrative.collector_notes: The dial is a matte black or silver with applied baton indices. The regulator sub-dial is at 6 with three sub-dials (day, date, month) and a sub-seconds.

narrative.story: The 5370P is the modern replacement for the 5004P. The CHR 29-535 PS caliber is the first Patek in-house column-wheel chronograph with a split-seconds mechanism; the column wheel is visible through the case back. The 41mm platinum case, the blue enamel dial, and the two-level sub-dial layout are the visual signature. The 5370P is the most-cited modern Patek grand complication chronograph and the watch a collector cites when arguing Patek's chronograph engineering is at the top of the Swiss industry.
narrative.collector_notes: The 5370P is the first Patek chronograph with a blue enamel dial; enamel is one of the most fragile dial-making processes and is hand-fired at 800°C.

identity.name: Rado Captain Cook 42

movement.caliber: Rado Caliber R763 (Sellita SW200-1 base, 80h reserve)

identity.one_liner: The Captain Cook 42 reissues the 1962 Rado dive watch — high-tech ceramic, 80h movement, and a bracelet that wears like a hot knife through rubber.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Wikimedia Commons — closest verified CC-licensed photo for the Rado Rado Captain Cook 42. Title: File:RADO Captain Cook Redition .jpg.

narrative.story: The original Captain Cook was issued in 1962, the same year as the first dive watches from Blancpain and Zodiac. The 2021 reissue takes the 1962 silhouette and the boxed sapphire crystal and pairs them with a modern Sellita-based 80-hour movement and Rado's signature high-tech ceramic bezel insert. Rado is the Swatch Group brand with the deepest ceramic-construction heritage — the Captain Cook is the watch the brand uses to demonstrate that ceramic can be made to look like a 1960s dive watch and not like a 2000s Apple Watch. The Captain Cook sells particularly well in Singapore and Bangkok, where Rado has long had brand recognition through its jewellery-watch sister line.
narrative.collector_notes: The 80-hour power reserve is the headline spec — it is one of the few sub-$2,500 Swiss dive watches with an 80h movement. The ceramic bezel is virtually scratch-proof. The bracelet uses a quick-change system; the rubber strap is included in the box and the bracelet-to-rubber swap takes about 30 seconds with no tools.

identity.one_liner: Rexhep Rexhepi's first watch under his own name, a hand-finished time-only piece with subsidiary seconds that established him as the reference point for the newest generation of independent watchmakers.

narrative.story: Rexhep Rexhepi trained under Patek Philippe and BNB (Vaucher's complications workshop) and briefly partnered in Akrivia before releasing the Chronomètre Contemporain in 2018 as the first watch carrying his own name on the dial. Built around a hand-finished manual movement with black-polished steel components and subsidiary seconds, the piece drew immediate comparisons to Philippe Dufour's Simplicity for its restraint and finishing quality, and within a few years of release was already appearing at major auction houses at multiples of its original retail price.
narrative.collector_notes: Case metal (pink gold, platinum, and later stainless steel) is the primary variant collectors track; steel examples are the rarest of the three and carry the largest premium.

identity.name: Automatic Extra Flat
identity.one_liner: The 38.7mm extra-flat Richard Mille — the brand's most wearable entry, designed with sprinter Wayde van Niekerk. Carbon-TPT case, 7.8mm thin, the RM that does not look like an RM.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Richard Mille Automatic Extra Flat (RM 67-02). Richard Mille RM 011 Felt. Verified CC-licensed photograph representing Richard Mille tonneau case architecture and NTPT carbon.

provenance_events.description: Richard Mille releases the 32-gram RM 67-02 sports watch with the automatic CRMA7 calibre.

narrative.story: The RM 67-02 is the most restrained Richard Mille in production. The 38.7mm tonneau case is 7.8mm thin — the thinnest RM ever. The CRMA7 caliber is a skeletonized micro-rotor automatic with a 50-hour reserve. The "Extra Flat" name is misleading; the watch is only extra flat by Richard Mille standards (most RM cases are 12-16mm thick). The RM 67-02 was the watch worn by sprinter Wayde van Niekerk in his post-injury comeback and the watch worn on the wrist of actress Margot Robbie in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. The RM 67-02 is the most-cited "wearable" Richard Mille and the only one a normal human can fit under a shirt cuff.

case.material: titanium (also produced in gold, ceramic, and carbon composites)

narrative.story: The RM 011 partnered Richard Mille with Felipe Massa, then racing for Ferrari, applying the brand's tonneau-case architecture to a chronograph rather than the tourbillons that had defined the marque's early output. The skeletonized dial and variable-geometry rotor were shown openly rather than hidden, which became a recognizable house signature across the RM catalog. The line has continued in numerous case materials and dial colorways well beyond its 2007 debut.

Buyers confirm the exact sub-reference against the movement serial before assuming a listing photo matches the described material.

identity.name: Explorer
identity.one_liner: The Explorer of 1963-1989: matte black dial, 3-6-9 numerals, 36mm, and a 26-year production run.

brand_context.label: Iconic mainstream leaders
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

media.caption: Rolex Explorer ref. 1016 — the longest-running Explorer (1963–1989). Worn by Jennifer Connelly's character in Top Gun: Maverick.

provenance_events.description: The Explorer 1016 runs from 1963 to 1989 — the longest-running Explorer reference and the one most associated with mountaineering expeditions, polar crossings, and 1970s-era tool-watch culture. The dial proportions and 36mm case became the template for every Rolex Explorer that followed.

screen_events.title: Rolex Explorer 1016 - Jennifer Connelly - Top Gun: Maverick
screen_events.description: Jennifer Connelly’s Penny in Top Gun: Maverick wears a vintage Explorer 1016 — the simple 3-6-9 explorer dial. A premiere still is credited below; the in-cockpit prop close-up stays with Paramount.

media.caption: Jennifer Connelly at the Top Gun: Maverick premiere, San Diego, May 2022 — the closest verified CC-licensed photograph of the actress in a public film context. The actual in-film watch-in-scene image is copyrighted by Paramount and is not available for free reuse.

narrative.story: The 1016 distilled the Explorer to its lasting form — matte black dial, luminous 3-6-9, calibers 1560 then 1570 — and held it for two and a half decades. Early gilt-dial examples and the rare 'Space-Dweller' variant sit at the top of the market, while later matte watches are the canonical entry into vintage sports Rolex. Its plainness is the point: one dial, one case, no date.

narrative.collector_notes: White 'panda' dials carry a consistent premium over black. Check the bezel edge for chips and the warranty-card date; 2023-dated full sets mark the final production year.

media.caption: The first Rolex Submariner from 1953. The closest verified CC-licensed photograph for the 1680 and 5513 family; the pictured watch is the original Submariner reference, the 1680 and 5513 are direct descendants.

provenance_events.description: The 1680 is the first Submariner Date, with a cyclops, and runs 1975-1979. The "Red Submariner" text below 6 o'clock identifies Mk1 examples and remains the most-cited variant among vintage Submariner Date collectors.

narrative.story: The 1680 added a date and cyclops to the Submariner, and early production printed the model name in red — a detail dropped around 1975 when the text turned white. narrative.story: The SKX007 ran caliber 7S26 — a 21-jewel automatic with no hacking seconds and no hand-winding — in a 42.5mm case with a 200m-rated screw-down crown and a unidirectional dive bezel. Introduced in 1996, it became the standard recommendation for a first automatic watch through the 2000s and 2010s on the strength of its price, durability, and ease of modification. Seiko discontinued the reference in 2019, a decision that drew sustained discussion across watch forums and pushed secondary-market prices above its original retail level.

media.license: Personal photograph, used with explicit consent. Not a free-reuse license. Shown as a self-referential test case for the register.
media.caption: Founder, 2005. The TAG Heuer Aquaracer 300M WAY101A on the wrist, in front of Taywin mall, Bangkok. A self-referential dossier: the only card whose owner is the system author.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Founder's father gifts the watch on the day the founder received his MIT admission letter
provenance_events.description: The watch was bought in Bangkok in July 2005. The founder's father, a technical engineer, was the one who taught him to read a movement by holding it up to the light. The photo in /about/founder-2005.jpg is from that day. The watch was worn through the founder's four years at MIT and through fifteen years of travel since. It has been serviced three times (battery, gaskets) and is still running. The 20-year battery life of the quartz movement is not an accident; it is the design.

narrative.story: This is the only watch on the founder's wrist. He is not a collector. He is a builder of systems for cities, and the Aquaracer 300M is what survives his travel. The reference WAY101A is the mid-2000s stainless steel three-hand, 43mm, with the black aluminum dive bezel, six-stud grip case, and 300m water resistance. It was bought for him in 2005 by his father on the day the founder was admitted to MIT. Twenty years later, the watch has been serviced three times (battery, gaskets) and is still running on the original quartz movement. It is included in the register because the system requires that its own author's watch be subject to the same evidence standard as every other reference on the site. The watch is rated attainable tier. The story is rated priceless; the register does not have a tier for that.
narrative.collector_notes: The WAY101A is the kind of object the system exists to protect: a watch with no auction comps, no premium over retail, no provenance events except the one above. It is in the register because it is the founder's watch, not because the system would otherwise have included it. Read it as the proof of the system, not as a recommendation.

identity.name: Monaco Chronograph Calibre 11
identity.one_liner: TAG Heuer's blue-dial automatic reissue of the square chronograph Steve McQueen wore in Le Mans (1971), since discontinued.

brand_context.label: Accessible luxury
brand_context.limitation: A subjective editorial map of craft, heritage, recognition, and demand. It is context only and never enters price, scarcity, or collectibility calculations.

provenance_events.description: The Heuer Monaco Steve McQueen gave to his Le Mans mechanic Haig Alltounian, caseback engraved "To Haig / Le Mans 1970," sells at Phillips New York for $2,208,000 including buyer's premium — a record for any Heuer or TAG Heuer chronograph at auction.

Jack Heuer designs the Monaco in 1969 — the first square-cased, water-resistant automatic chronograph. Steve McQueen wears it in Le Mans (1971), turning the Monaco into TAG Heuer's most-photographed vintage reference. Reissued 1998, 2003, 2009, 2015; the Calibre 11 reissue (CAW211P) runs 2015-2023.

narrative.story: Heuer introduced the Monaco in 1969 as one of the first automatic chronographs, built around a square case with the crown on the left side. Steve McQueen wore a blue-dial Heuer Monaco on-screen as racing driver Michael Delaney in the 1971 film Le Mans, and the model he later gave his personal mechanic sold at Phillips in December 2020 for $2,208,000, a record for the brand at auction. TAG Heuer's modern Calibre 11 reissue, ref. CAW211P, revived the blue dial and left-side crown on a 39mm case before being discontinued.
narrative.collector_notes: The 39mm case reads small next to contemporary chronographs, and the left-side crown takes some adjustment; check which Calibre 11-generation dial print (TAG Heuer vs. Heuer branding, date-window position) matches the specific reference before buying pre-owned.

identity.name: Oyster Prince Submariner
identity.one_liner: Tudor's first Submariner without crown guards, identified by an oversized winding crown relative to its thin case, which gave the reference its 'Big Crown' name among collectors.

brand_context.label: Accessible luxury

provenance_events.description: Tudor produces the 7924 Oyster Prince Submariner from 1958-1968 as Tudor's first Submariner. The 7924 is the basis of the French Navy issue Tudor Submariners of the 1960s and a Hong Kong vintage-market staple.

narrative.story: Tudor's first Submariner-family divers, launched in 1954 as the Oyster Prince Submariner, initially had no crown guards, leaving the winding crown exposed at the case side. Reference 7924, made in 1958-59, is the last of that crown-guard-less generation before Tudor added guards with reference 7928, and its oversized crown relative to the thin case gave it the 'Big Crown' name collectors use today. The Black Bay Fifty-Eight, launched six decades later, takes its case proportions directly from this reference.
narrative.collector_notes: Because 7924 was produced for only about a year before Tudor moved to the crown-guarded 7928, unmolested examples with matching dial, hands, and bezel insert are scarce; buyers check crown diameter, dial print generation, and bezel material closely against known reference photos before purchase.

provenance_events.description: Vacheron put the Historiques 222 into stainless steel (ref. 4200H/222A-B934) at $32,000 — the configuration collectors had asked for since the 2022 yellow-gold reissue, and the closest thing to the original 1977 steel 222 the modern catalog offers.

Vacheron Constantin's 222 — designed by Jörg Hysek — launches for the brand's 222nd anniversary. A 37mm gold integrated bracelet with a notched bezel at 5 o'clock, the 222 is the third of the "Holy Trinity" sports watches after the Royal Oak (1972) and Nautilus (1976).

Vacheron Constantin reissues the 222 as the Historiques 222 ref. 4200H/222, a 37mm yellow-gold faithful reissue with a "Jubilee"-style bracelet — the spiritual sibling to the 1972 Royal Oak and 1976 Nautilus reissues.

Vacheron Constantin reissues the 222 as the Historiques 222 ref. 4200H/222, a 37mm yellow-gold faithful reissue with a "Jubilee"-style bracelet. The reissue is the brand's biggest launch of the 2020s in Asia — Hong Kong collector circles form the core of the buy-in list.

narrative.story: The 222 was Vacheron's 1977 entry in the integrated-bracelet race — designed not by Genta but by a 24-year-old Jorg Hysek for the maison's 222nd anniversary, with a notched tonneau bezel and a small gold Maltese cross set into the case flank at 5 o'clock. The 2022 Historiques reissue in yellow gold reproduced it at 37mm almost line for line, down to the flank cross, on the modern caliber 2455/2. The steel version followed in 2025 at $32,000, and vintage 222s have been repriced upward in its wake.
narrative.collector_notes: Reissue versus vintage is the whole conversation: the 4200H is a modern watch with a sapphire back and current water resistance, while original 44018 examples carry the collector premium. On the reissue, check the flank Maltese cross and bracelet taper for damage — both are expensive to make right.
