identity.name: Observatoire
identity.nickname: Fifty observatory movements, found on a shelf

case.material: 18k white gold, also issued in stainless steel and platinum

identity.one_liner: Kari Voutilainen found a batch of observatory-grade Peseux calibres that had been fabricated but never assembled, and built his first watch around them. About fifty exist. It won the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève in the year it launched, and it was gone by 2011.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève, Best Men's Watch
provenance_events.description: The Observatoire was introduced in 2007 and awarded Best Men's Watch at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève that same year. It was Voutilainen's first watch built around a movement he had not designed himself, and the only one of its kind.

The Observatoire was discontinued in 2011 and replaced by the Vingt-8, which carried Voutilainen's own in-house calibre 28. The model ran for roughly four years and approximately fifty pieces were made.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Phillips New York Watch Auction: XIV, lot 82
provenance_events.description: Case no. C260101, a 2009 white gold example, was sold for USD 1,041,400 against an estimate of USD 100,000-200,000.

narrative.story:
Voutilainen spent his career building movements. The Observatoire is the exception, and that is the whole story.

The occasion was luck rather than design. Kari Voutilainen came across a group of Peseux calibres that had been fabricated but never assembled — observatory-grade movements, mid-twentieth century, of a quality that was never going to be put on sale to the public. They were components, not watches. He decided to build a small series around them.

What came out was a 38-to-39mm dress watch with tear-drop lugs, a gold guilloché dial, a free-sprung Glycydur balance and gold hands, on a movement of 30mm and 21 jewels that he did not design and could not have designed: a regulator-grade calibre for measuring time, repurposed to tell it. Phillips records that only around 3,300 examples of that movement were ever made and that it was never available for public purchase, which is precisely the point of finding one on a shelf.

It won Best Men's Watch at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève in 2007, the year it launched. It ran for about four years and roughly fifty pieces, in white gold, stainless steel and platinum, and then Voutilainen did the sensible thing and put his own calibre 28 inside a new watch — the Vingt-8 — which is where the rest of this register's Voutilainen cards come from.

The New York example that sold in June 2026 is case C260101, a 2009 watch in white gold. It made $1,041,400 against an estimate of $100,000 to $200,000.
narrative.collector_notes:
Two measurement conventions exist for the case and this dossier does not paper over them. Examples from 2008 are published at 38mm — including Voutilainen's own authorised retailer, whose spec sheet lists a 38.00mm case and a 30.00mm movement. The 2009 example recorded here measures 39mm. The dossier carries 39mm because that is the measurement on the lot on file; a collector comparing an earlier example should expect the 38mm figure instead.

Only one dated sale is imported here. Phillips has offered the Observatoire repeatedly — an 18k white gold 2008 example at USD 215,900 in New York, and a stainless steel 2009 example at CHF 381,000 in its Decade One sale — but those sale dates are not in this register's harvest, so those figures are named and left out rather than dated approximately.

No maker list price is on file. Marketplace asking prices for the Observatoire cluster between roughly USD 61,000 and USD 75,000, but an aggregator's asking price is not a published MSRP and is not entered as one.

produced.end_year_note: Voutilainen discontinued the Vingt-8 Inverse after a run of 26 pieces and has never published the year it stopped. Phillips states only that the reference is discontinued; the last dated example on record here was made in 2020.

case.material: platinum, also issued in tantalum and titanium

identity.one_liner: Voutilainen turned his own movement back to front: the escapement and balance that the Vingt-8 hides behind a caseback sit on top of the dial instead, which cost the calibre an indirect gear train so the hands could still run clockwise. Twenty-six were made, in three metals that have almost no resale market between them.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève, Men's Watch Prize
provenance_events.description: The Vingt-8 Inversé was introduced in 2019 and received the Men's Watch Prize at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève the same year.
The example sold in New York in 2026 was guaranteed in December 2020 and comes with its servicing history booklet, placing it among the first pieces off the line rather than at the end of the run.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Phillips New York Watch Auction: XIV, lot 9
provenance_events.description: Movement no. 28Pi-5, one of eight platinum examples, was sold for USD 1,155,700 after 15 bids — roughly five to six times the top of its estimate. Phillips records it as part of a season in which independent watchmaking was the leading story of the sale.

narrative.story:
The Vingt-8 shows you a dial and hides its movement. The Inversé swaps the two and dares you to read it.

Kari Voutilainen introduced the Vingt-8 in 2011 around a calibre 28 he designed himself, and put the escapement and its oversized balance under a caseback where you could admire them in private. In 2019 he reversed the whole thing for the Vingt-8 Inversé: the movement is displayed on the dial side, the part you normally hide is the part you cannot avoid, and the watch asks whether that still counts as a watch.

It very nearly did not work. Turning the calibre over would have reversed the direction the gears turned, and a watch whose hands run anticlockwise is not a watch. Voutilainen re-engineered it around an indirect gear train at the centre of the dial — visible, because everything is visible here — so the hands would still travel clockwise the way a wrist expects. The centre of the dial is therefore a mechanical answer to a mechanical objection, and it is the best part of the watch.

There were twenty-six. Ten in tantalum, eight in titanium, eight in platinum. No steel, no gold, no two configurations the secondary market has ever learned to price. Then it was discontinued.

It won the Men's Watch Prize at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève in the year it launched. The platinum example Phillips sold in New York in June 2026 was guaranteed in December 2020, carries movement number 28Pi-5, and made $1,155,700 after fifteen bids against a top estimate of $200,000. Phillips put it down as property of the original owner's family, and flagged that it had not been tested for timekeeping and may want a service.

One of eight. None of the other seven will be easy to find, and none of the eighteen non-platinum pieces has an obvious buyer waiting for it. That asymmetry is the actual investment story: the metal is the scarce part, and the market has not yet learned to separate the two.
narrative.collector_notes:
Two cautions sit on this dossier on purpose. First, the seller is the original owner's family, so provenance is a single line rather than a chain; second, Phillips states the watch was not tested for timekeeping accuracy and may require a service at the buyer's expense. Neither is a defect. Both change what the number means, and a $1.16M hammer-adjacent result on an untested, family-held example is not the same as a result on a serviced, documented one.

No maker list price is on file. The run is documented and the metals are documented; the price Voutilainen charged is not, and an aggregator's asking price is not entered as one.

The tantalum example Phillips offered for Geneva in November 2026 is described in the house's own catalogue note as a unique commission engraved '1/1', with its ring and hand colours specified for that watch. That is a one-off, not a ninth platinum piece, and it is not what this card represents.

identity.name: Vingt-8 ISO
identity.one_liner: The Vingt-8 ISO keeps Voutilainen's calibre 28 but changes how the dial is read: the hour hand turns once every twelve hours while the minute hand turns thirteen times an hour, so the time comes from the two hands' relation to each other, not from a glance.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

provenance_events.description: Phillips dates lot 140 to circa 2017 and records that the ISO's rotating display required a newly configured movement, slightly thicker than the standard Caliber 28.

The Phillips lot offered in New York in June 2026 carries a Voutilainen certificate booklet dated February 2017 and movement number 28ISO-2, which Phillips reads as likely the second ISO Voutilainen built.

provenance_events.person_or_event: Phillips New York Watch Auction: XIV, lot 140
provenance_events.description: The Vingt-8 ISO offered as lot 140 sold for USD 1,206,500 against an estimate of USD 100,000-200,000, about six times the high estimate. The sale was held 13-14 June 2026; Phillips calls this likely the 2nd Vingt-8 ISO ever made and the 2nd sold by the house.

narrative.story:
The Vingt-8 ISO changes what a dial asks of you. Phillips says its display takes inspiration from the psychologist Daniel Kahneman's account of two ways the brain forms thoughts: System 1, fast and intuitive, and System 2, slow and deliberate. Reading a regular watch is System 1. The ISO is built to make the wearer engage with time differently. The hour hand turns at the normal 12-hour speed while the minute hand turns 13 times every hour. At the full hour the two hands overlap; at every half hour they sit exactly opposite; at the quarter hours they are 90 degrees apart. The time is read from the hands in relation to each other, not against the minute scale on the outer ring.

The movement is Voutilainen's own. Phillips describes the Caliber 28 as using two escape wheels that deliver direct impulses to a sizeable balance wheel, reducing friction compared with a traditional Swiss lever escapement. European Watch describes a free-sprung balance with a Breguet overcoil and a Grossman spiral. The rotating display needed a newly configured movement, slightly thicker than the standard Caliber 28; the watch Phillips sold carries 35 jewels.

The sale is the evidence about how rare it is. Phillips calls lot 140 likely the 2nd Vingt-8 ISO ever made, judging from its movement number, 28ISO-2, and only the 2nd sold by Phillips. It carried an estimate of USD 100,000 to 200,000 and sold for USD 1,206,500. Phillips also says the St-Sulpice manufacture still produces fewer than 60 pieces per year.
narrative.collector_notes: No retail price is on file for the ISO, so this register carries an empty MSRP history rather than a borrowed one. The only sale on file is the Phillips New York lot, one data point, so no market value is computed. Scarcity here rests on the brand-level production figure alone (fewer than 60 pieces a year, per Phillips); the register has no evidence that the ISO is a numbered or limited edition.

identity.name: El Primero A386 Revival
identity.one_liner: A close reissue of the 1969 A386 — the original case housing the El Primero, the movement that gave Zenith its claim to the first automatic chronograph.

brand_context.limitation: This brand is not classified in the cited editorial tier framework.

media.caption: Vintage Zenith El Primero A385 (1970s) — the tri-color sub-dial layout the modern A386 Revival reproduces. The 1969 A386 was Zenith's first El Primero execution.

provenance_events.description: Zenith launches the El Primero inside the A386, described by the brand as the first high-frequency automatic chronograph movement, running at 36,000 vibrations per hour against the 18,000–21,600 vph typical of the era.

narrative.story: The El Primero has since been credited, alongside the Heuer-Breitling-Hamilton 'Chronomatic' Caliber 11 and Seiko's Caliber 6139, as one of three roughly simultaneous claimants to the first automatic chronograph movement — a race horological histories still argue over rather than settle. During the mid-1970s quartz crisis, Zenith's then-owners ordered the El Primero's production tooling scrapped as the brand pivoted to quartz; watchmaker Charles Vermot hid the tooling and technical plans in the attic of the manufacture in Le Locle instead of destroying them. When demand for mechanical chronographs returned in the 1980s — including from Rolex, which used a modified El Primero as the base of its own Daytona movement from 1988 to 2000 — Vermot's hidden tooling let Zenith restart El Primero production rather than redesign the caliber from nothing.
narrative.collector_notes: Compare the lume plot and dial printing closely against the specific vintage reference a given 'revival' claims to reissue — Zenith has released several A386-cased tricolor models over the years with small but collector-relevant differences in case finishing and dial text versus the actual 1969 original.
